summary: Specifies the Trivial File Transfer Protocol, a very simple protocol for moving files between hosts. This second revision was later replaced. Replaced by RFC 1350.

eli5.summary: A very simple way to copy a file from one computer to another, like passing a note with no extras. Later a newer version took over.

questions: when to use tftp instead of ftp
subtitle: A very simple protocol for transferring files between computers

tldr.problem: Regular FTP is complex and requires authentication, directory listing, and other features. Some applications need a minimal file transfer mechanism that can be implemented quickly and easily.
tldr.mechanism: TFTP runs on top of UDP and implements only the core file read and write operations, using fixed 512-byte blocks with lock-step acknowledgment, three transfer modes (netascii, octet, and mail), and simple error handling.
tldr.outcome: TFTP became widely deployed for simple tasks like diskless system bootstrapping, but it was later superseded by RFC 1350, which provides a more robust specification.

today: RFC 783 is historic. It was superseded by RFC 1350, which provides the standard specification for TFTP and remains in use today for simple file transfer in network boot and embedded systems.

sections.title: A Trivial File Transfer Protocol
sections.content:
TFTP is a very simple protocol designed for transferring files between machines on different networks. It is implemented on top of UDP, the Internet User Datagram Protocol, so it works on any network that supports UDP.

TFTP is intentionally minimal. It can only read and write files (or mail), and it cannot list directories or authenticate users. This simplicity makes it easy to implement in small programs and firmware, particularly for bootstrapping diskless systems or embedded devices.
sections.eli5: TFTP is a simple way to copy a file from one computer to another. It only does file copy, nothing fancy.

sections.title: Packets and Operation
sections.content:
TFTP transfers files in fixed blocks of 512 bytes. Files are transferred using five types of packets: Read Request (RRQ) and Write Request (WRQ) to start a transfer, Data (DATA) packets containing file blocks, Acknowledgment (ACK) packets confirming receipt, and Error (ERROR) packets signaling problems.

Each end of the connection chooses a Transfer ID (TID), a random port number between 0 and 65,535, used for the duration of the transfer. The client initiates requests to the well-known port 69 on the server. The server responds using a different TID to continue the transfer.

TFTP uses lock-step acknowledgment: each data block must be acknowledged before the next block can be sent. If a block is lost, the sender times out and retransmits it.
sections.eli5: Files break into chunks of 512 bytes. One computer sends a chunk, the other says 'got it', and then the next chunk goes. If something gets lost, it is sent again.

sections.title: Transfer Modes
sections.content:
TFTP supports three transfer modes. Netascii is ASCII text with line ending conversions for compatibility across different systems. Octet is raw 8-bit binary data transferred without transformation. Mail works like netascii but sends the data to a mail recipient instead of a file, using a recipient name in the format 'username' or 'username@hostname'.

Implementations can define additional modes for cooperating hosts, but no central authority defines or assigns these modes.
sections.eli5: TFTP can send text files (converting line endings), binary files (without changes), or mail messages. Custom modes are allowed for special cases.
